citations.quote: Let $c>0$, $0\le v_*<c$, and $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for all $s$. For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ there is exactly one real root $s=s(x,t)$ of $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and $s\le t$. Equality holds exactly when $x=z(t)$. Thus on the open off-instantaneous-worldline domain $D=\{(x,t):x\ne z(t)\}$ one has $s<t$, $r=|x-z(s)|=c(t-s)>0$, and the root is $C^1$. With $n=(x-z(s))/r$, $\beta=z'(s)/c$, and $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$, its derivatives are $\partial_t s=1/\kappa$ and $\nabla_xs=-n/(c\kappa)$, where $1-v_*/c\le\kappa\le1+v_*/c$. If $z$ is $C^k$, for an integer $k\ge1$, the root is $C^k$ on $D$; in particular a $C^3$ trajectory gives a $C^3$ root. A smooth trajectory gives a smooth root. No higher regularity follows from a merely $C^1$ trajectory. These claims concern an all-time uniformly subluminal prescribed history; no finite-history or nonuniform-light-speed-limit assertion is made.

is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.**

A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

**Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.

**Proper-graph branch.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $z:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^1$ trajectory, put $\gamma(t):=(z(t),t)$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be open with $\gamma[I]\subseteq\Omega$. Assume the graph map $\gamma:I\to\Omega$ is **proper**: $\gamma^{-1}[K]$ is a compact subset of $I$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. For $q\in\mathbb R$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle:=q\int_I\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,\qquad \langle J,\psi\rangle:=q\int_I z'(t)\,\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,$$

the second integral being componentwise, so $J=(J_1,J_2,J_3)$ is a triple of distributions, with components $\langle J_i,\psi\rangle=q\int_Iz_i'(t)\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$. Then $\rho$ and $J$ are distributions on $\Omega$ ([[def-distribution]]) and, with the distributional derivative of [[def-distributional-derivative]],

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Omega).$$

Complex integrals mean $\int w:=\int\operatorname{Re}w+i\int\operatorname{Im}w$, with the same componentwise convention for improper limits. In formulas involving complex tests, $\langle u,w\rangle:=\sum_{j=1}^3u_jw_j$ for $u\in\mathbb R^3$ and $w\in\mathbb C^3$, with no conjugation. This extends the real coordinate pairing; estimates on $J$ mean estimates on each component.

In the proper branch, an integral over $I$ means the proper integral over any compact subinterval containing the pulled-back support, with the integrand zero near its ends; additivity makes this independent of the subinterval. For $I=\varnothing$ both functionals are defined to be zero. Properness is automatic if $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, and also if $I=\mathbb R$.

**Endpoint branch.** Suppose instead that $I=(a,b)$ is bounded with finite endpoints, that $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, that the absolute improper integral $\int_a^b\lVert z'(t)\rVert_2\,dt$ is finite, and that both endpoint events $(z(a),a)$ and $(z(b),b)$ belong to $\Omega$. Then the same formulas, with the integrals understood as improper integrals over $(a,b)$, define distributions $\rho$ and $J$ on $\Omega$, and

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\,\delta_{(z(a),a)}-q\,\delta_{(z(b),b)},$$

the Dirac distributions being those of [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]].

Mere graph containment $\gamma[I]\subseteq\Omega$ does not make the pulled-back tests compactly supported, and it does not by itself give the source-free identity: in the endpoint branch the endpoint terms are exactly as displayed. Each individual endpoint contribution vanishes on a test if and only if $q=0$ or that test vanishes at the corresponding endpoint event. Their total pairing vanishes if and only if $q=0$ or $\psi(z(a),a)=\psi(z(b),b)$. No Maxwell equation, no point self-force and no physical interpretation of $\rho$ or $J$ is asserted; only the distributional identities for the prescribed support are proved.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), used through the sphere and polar integrations below ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]). Let $c>0$, write $Q:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, $\mathcal D:=\mathcal D(Q)$ for the test-function space of [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], and $C:=\{(y,t)\in Q:t=|y|/c\}$ for the retarded cone. Define the functional $K$ on test functions by

$$\langle K,\psi\rangle:=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\psi(y,|y|/c)}{|y|}\,dy\qquad(\psi\in\mathcal D).$$

Then: (a) the integral converges absolutely for every $\psi\in\mathcal D$, the functional $K$ is a distribution on $Q$ ([[def-distribution]]), $(K,\psi)=0$ for every $\psi$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap C=\varnothing$, and for every $(y_0,t_0)\in C$ and every neighbourhood $U$ of $(y_0,t_0)$ there is $\psi\in\mathcal D$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq U$ and $\langle K,\psi\rangle\ne0$; consequently $\operatorname{supp}K=C$. (b) For every $h\in C_c^\infty(Q)$ the function

$$(K*h)(x,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{h(y,\,t-|x-y|/c)}{4\pi\,|x-y|}\,dy$$

is well defined (the integral converges absolutely), of class $C^\infty$ on $Q$, and for every $\psi\in\mathcal D$

$$\langle K*h,\psi\rangle=\langle h,\,K\circledast\psi\rangle,\qquad (K\circledast\psi)(y,s):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,s+\cdot)\rangle=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\frac{\psi(y+z,s+|z|/c)}{|z|}\,dz;$$

moreover $W(K*h)=h$ on $Q$ in the classical pointwise sense, where $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ is the wave expression of [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]] and [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. (c) Read $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ as the distributional operator built from [[def-distributional-derivative]]; then $WK=\delta_{(0,0)}$ in the sense of [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]], that is, $(WK)(\psi)=\psi(0,0)$ for every $\psi\in\mathcal D$. This identifies $K$ as the retarded fundamental solution of $W$; no smoothness of $K$ itself on the cone is asserted, and the advanced fundamental solution is not treated.

(b) Let $K$ be the retarded wave kernel of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]] and, for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and $\tau\in\mathbb R$, $y\in\mathbb R^3$, put $(K\circledast\psi)(y,\tau):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,\tau+\cdot)\rangle$. Define the retarded-history pairings by the explicit integrals

$$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle:=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R}(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle:=\mu_0q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds.$$

Here the second integral is componentwise. The notation $\varepsilon_0^{-1}\langle\rho,K\circledast\psi\rangle$ and $\mu_0\langle J,K\circledast\psi\rangle$, if used, means precisely these explicit history integrals, rather than ordinary distribution action on a compactly supported test. These pairings define distributions on $\Omega$, are finite for every $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and satisfy the exact retarded-convolution identities

$$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{\beta(x,t)}{c}\,\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt$$

(for $\Upsilon$, componentwise against $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$; both integrands are continuous on the open set $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ and integrable there against $\psi$). Consequently the potentials are the $C^2$ functions

$$\varphi:=\frac{C}{D}=\frac{C}{\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R,\qquad A:=\frac{\beta\,\varphi}{c}=\frac{\beta\,C}{c\,\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R^3$$

off the worldline, and the zero extensions $\widetilde\varphi,\widetilde A$ on $\Gamma$ belong to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$; $\Phi$ is the regular distribution of $\widetilde\varphi$, and $\Upsilon$ that of $\widetilde A$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]).

(c) Let $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]). Then, off the worldline,

$$E=C\left[\frac{(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)}{\kappa^3r^2}+\frac{n\times\bigl((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta\bigr)}{c\,\kappa^3r}\right],\qquad B=\frac{n\times E}{c}.$$

The fields $E,B$ are $C^1$ off the worldline. More generally, if $z\in C^k$, $k\ge3$, the retarded root is $C^k$, the potentials are $C^{k-1}$ and the fields are $C^{k-2}$ there; if $z\in C^\infty$, all these objects are smooth off the worldline. The result is a mathematical model computation for the stipulated uniformly subluminal smooth worldline and the retarded choice; no self-force law, no radiation-reaction postulate and no physical Maxwell coupling is asserted or proved.

its **electric field** and **magnetic field** are

$$E(\varphi,A):=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. Both $E(\varphi,A)$ and $B(\varphi,A)$ are maps $\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**.
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

The **wave operator** of speed $c$ is
$$\Box_c:=\partial_t^2-c^2\Delta ,$$
and the **wave equation with source** $f$ is the equation $\Box_cu=f$ on a slab $\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$; the equation is **homogeneous** when $f=0$.

the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$.

A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Finite componentwise sums and products of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$, and a composite of composable $C^k$ Euclidean maps is $C^k$. Scalar multiples are included among the finite componentwise operations.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.**

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

Let $c>0$, $0\le v_*<c$, and $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for all $s$. For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ there is exactly one real root $s=s(x,t)$ of $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and $s\le t$. Equality holds exactly when $x=z(t)$. Thus on the open off-instantaneous-worldline domain $D=\{(x,t):x\ne z(t)\}$ one has $s<t$, $r=|x-z(s)|=c(t-s)>0$, and the root is $C^1$. With $n=(x-z(s))/r$, $\beta=z'(s)/c$, and $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$, its derivatives are $\partial_t s=1/\kappa$ and $\nabla_xs=-n/(c\kappa)$, where $1-v_*/c\le\kappa\le1+v_*/c$. If $z$ is $C^k$, for an integer $k\ge1$, the root is $C^k$ on $D$; in particular a $C^3$ trajectory gives a $C^3$ root. A smooth trajectory gives a smooth root. No higher regularity follows from a merely $C^1$ trajectory. These claims concern an all-time uniformly subluminal prescribed history; no finite-history or nonuniform-light-speed-limit assertion is made.

(a) [Root and emission-time Jacobian] For every $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ (equivalently $x\ne z(t)$) there is exactly one $s=s(x,t)<t$ with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$. The map $s:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ is of class $C^3$, and with $R:=x-z(s)$, $r:=|R|$, $n:=R/r$, $\beta:=z'(s)/c$ and $\kappa:=1-n\cdot\beta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) one has $$\partial_ts(x,t)=\kappa^{-1},\qquad \nabla_xs(x,t)=-\frac{n}{c\,\kappa},\qquad \kappa\in[1-v_*/c,\,1+v_*/c],$$ so $\kappa\ge 1-v_*/c>0$ uniformly on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$. Moreover, for the fixed $x$ and near the root, the function $s'\mapsto s'+|x-z(s')|/c$ is differentiable at $s'=s$ with derivative $\kappa(x,t)$: this emission-time Jacobian $1-n\cdot\beta$ is the denominator produced by the delta substitution of clause (b).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), used through the cited published suppliers ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, $t_0\in\mathbb R$, $T>t_0$, let $a,b\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and let $h\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T])$ in the extension sense that $h$ is the restriction of a $C^\infty$ function on $\mathbb R^3\times J$ for some open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Write $W:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$, so that $c^2W=\Box_c$ is the wave operator of speed $c$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]]). For $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and $s\ge0$ let $H_\varphi(x,s):=s\,M_{cs}\varphi(x)$, where $M_r\varphi(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{S^2}\varphi(x+rn)\,d\Omega(n)$ is the spherical mean of [[lem-em-spherical-mean-wave-identity]]. Define, with $s=t-t_0$, $$u(x,t):=\partial_sH_a(x,s)+H_b(x,s)+c^2\int_{t_0}^{t}H_{h(\cdot,v)}(x,t-v)\,dv,\qquad (x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T],$$ where $h(\cdot,v)$ denotes the map $x\mapsto h(x,v)$ and $\partial_sH_a$ is the partial derivative of $H_a$ in its second argument, evaluated at $s=t-t_0$. Then:

(a) $u$ is of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense, $Wu=h$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$ (indeed on the open neighbourhood of the closed time interval on which the extension of $h$ is defined), $u(\cdot,t_0)=a$ and $\partial_tu(\cdot,t_0)=b$.

(b) Uniqueness: every $v\in C^2(\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T])$ in the extension sense with $Wv=h$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$, $v(\cdot,t_0)=a$ and $\partial_tv(\cdot,t_0)=b$ equals $u$.

(c) Domain of dependence: let $\tilde a,\tilde b\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, $\tilde h\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T])$ and let $\tilde u$ be the corresponding solution. If $\tilde a=a$ and $\tilde b=b$ on the closed ball $\overline B_{c(t_*-t_0)}(x_*)$ and $\tilde h=h$ on the closed backward cone $K(x_*,t_*):=\{(y,v)\in\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,t_*]:|y-x_*|\le c(t_*-v)\}$ ([[def-forward-and-backward-wave-cones-domain-of-dependence-and-influence]]), then $\tilde u(x_*,t_*)=u(x_*,t_*)$ for every $x_*\in\mathbb R^3$ and $t_*\in[t_0,T]$.

(d) Compact support: if $a$ vanishes off a compact $K_a\subset\mathbb R^3$, $b$ vanishes off a compact $K_b$, and $h(\cdot,v)$ vanishes off a fixed compact $K_h$ for every $v\in[t_0,T]$, then for every $t\in[t_0,T]$ the function $u(\cdot,t)$ has compact spatial support: if $K_a\cup K_b\cup K_h\subseteq\overline B_\rho(0)$ for some $\rho>0$ (which exists, [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]), then $u(x,t)=0$ whenever $|x|>\rho+c(t-t_0)$.

No boundary condition on a finite spatial domain, no finite-total-energy hypothesis, and no decay of $a,b,h$ at infinity is assumed or asserted.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $n\ge1$, $c>0$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$
be an open interval and let $u:U\times I\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$
([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]). Write
$u_t:=\partial_tu$ and let

$$Du:=(\partial_0u,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}u)$$

be the spatial gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], a $C^1$ field
$U\times I\to\mathbb R^n$ whose Euclidean norm is $|Du|$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

The **kinetic density**, **potential density** and **energy density** of $u$ are
the continuous functions

$$e_{\mathrm{kin}}:=\frac12u_t^2,\qquad e_{\mathrm{pot}}:=\frac{c^2}{2}|Du|^2,\qquad e:=e_{\mathrm{kin}}+e_{\mathrm{pot}}=\frac12\bigl(u_t^2+c^2|Du|^2\bigr),$$

and the **energy flux** is the $C^1$ vector field

$$q:=-c^2u_t\,Du$$

([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). For a Lebesgue-measurable
$\Omega\subseteq U$ and a time $t\in I$ with
$\int_\Omega e(x,t)\,dx<\infty$, the **total energy in $\Omega$** is the real
number

$$E_\Omega(t):=\int_\Omega e(x,t)\,dx$$

([[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]); when the integral is infinite the total
energy is $+\infty$ and no real value is assigned.

**Sign convention.** If $\Omega$ is admissible for the divergence theorem with
outward unit normal $\nu$, then $\int_{\partial\Omega}q\cdot\nu\,dS$ is the
energy leaving $\Omega$ across $\partial\Omega$ per unit time. This is the
convention under which the pointwise identity
$\partial_te+\operatorname{div}q=u_t\,\Box_cu$ of
[[lem-local-wave-energy-conservation-law]] holds with
$\Box_c=\partial_t^2-c^2\Delta$
([[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]]): the flux vector
$q=-c^2u_tDu$ points in the direction of energy transport, and
$\operatorname{div}q$ is the local rate at which energy leaves a point.

**Speed convention.** The gradient term carries the exact factor $c^2$, so at
unit speed the energy density is the familiar
$\frac12u_t^2+\frac12|Du|^2$ and the flux is $-u_tDu$. The general-speed
statements of this page are rendered at $c>0$ throughout.

No equation for $u$, no finiteness of a particular integral and no regularity of
any boundary are asserted here: each statement that uses these objects states
its own hypotheses, and sufficient settings in which $E_\Omega$ is finite and constant
are supplied by [[thm-conservation-of-total-wave-energy]].
